transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-04-11 15:00 UTC — Duration: 40m. Attendees: Ava (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Samir (Redwood SE), Jen (CSM), Maya (Aperture ML Lead), Omar (Infra), Lisa (PM), Ethan (SRE).

Summary: Quick review of week 2 pilot quantization results. Focus on observed perf deltas (throughput/latency), quality regressions in generative tasks, weird failure modes on long-context prompts, and a concrete fallback/rollout plan. Agreed to run a larger FP8 stability sweep and provide logits traces for debugging.

Topics: 1) INT8 vs FP8 numeric deltas and perf, 2) quality-impact concrete examples, 3) calibration strategy and per-layer knobs, 4) rollout + automatic fallback to FP16, 5) next steps / who owns what.

[00:00:12] Ava (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro — we'll run through the numbers Diego pulled, show the sample failures, and map next steps. Maya, anything to add at the top?

[00:00:28] Maya (Aperture): No, this is perfect. We want to understand whether FP8 is safe enough to push into canary for our summarization flow — we care a lot about hallucinations on long docs.

[00:00:42] Diego (Redwood SE): Cool. I'll start with the bench numbers. This is a mixed workload — 65% generation (summaries), 25% chat-ish completions, 10% embeddings. Baseline is FP16 running on p4-like nodes.

[00:01:05] Diego: INT8 — after layerwise symmetric quant + per-channel activation clip calibration, we saw about 2.6x peak token throughput and steady-state about 2.2x under our continuous-batching profile. Median p95 latency per-token dropped ~28%. FP8 — using the new dynamic exponent format we tested — gave ~3.1x peak throughput and ~35% p95 latency reduction versus FP16.

[00:01:35] Omar (Aperture): Wait, 3.1x for FP8? That's a big win. What's the memory footprint delta?

[00:01:44] Diego: Memory wise INT8 cuts model memory roughly ~2x; FP8 sits in between — about 1.7x reduction versus FP16 because of format overhead in our runtime. These are ballpark numbers across the batch sizes we tried.

[00:01:58] Samir (Redwood SE): Important to highlight: FP8 was faster but more brittle on generative quality for some prompts. We instrumented with perplexity and a human-acceptability metric — the latter is a small-scale rubrikized judge run.

[00:02:16] Lisa (PM): Can you quantify brittle? We need numbers we can take to stakeholders.

[00:02:23] Diego: Sure — on the 500-sample business prompt set: INT8 had a mean acceptability drop of about 1.8 percentage points (baseline 92.6% -> 90.8%). FP8 had a larger drop: about 3.7 points (92.6% -> 88.9%). For rouge-like metrics on extractive summarization the delta was smaller: ~1-2% relative.

[00:02:50] Maya: Hmm, 3.7 points could be material. Were these short prompts or long context?

[00:02:57] Diego: FP8 failures clustered in long-context (>1k tokens) generative cases. We saw more token-level drift late in output — repetition and factual flip errors. For short prompts FP8 matched FP16 more closely. INT8's regressions were more evenly distributed but smaller in magnitude.

[00:03:20] Ethan (SRE): Do you have example transcripts? It helps to triage.

[00:03:24] Samir: Yes, we captured 12 representative failures. Example: prompt about quarterly revenue — FP16 summary: "Revenue up 6% QoQ due to X". FP8 summary: "Revenue down 6% QoQ due to X" — sign flip, probably numerical attenuation problem on a late token. The logits trace shows low confidence at the flip token.

[00:03:51] Maya: Oof. That's exactly the kind of risk. If FP8 introduces sign flips on numeric summaries, we can't ship without strong mitigations.

[00:03:59] Diego: Agreed. That's why we recommend a canary with automatic fallback. Our suggested rollout: start with 5% traffic on FP8 for short-context routes only, keep long-context pinned to INT8 or FP16, monitor acceptability and a small set of business checks, and automatically route to FP16 if a model-level quality alarm is tripped for >0.5% of requests in 5m.

[00:04:25] Ava: To add, we can use Redwood Optimize to suggest per-route quant profiles: e.g., use per-layer higher-precision for attention heads in early layers which seemed correlated with drift. Also prefix/KV cache behavior matters — we saw KV cache serialization differences when we switched quant formats (KV cash in one of the transcriptions — lol).

[00:04:49] Omar: Is the fallback quick? What's the latency cost when we fallback to FP16?

[00:04:53] Samir: Fallback is an immediate route change — if the canary triggers, traffic for matching sessions will be routed to FP16 variants. Cold-start latency can be 3-12s for a new replica if capacity isn't pre-warmed. We recommend keeping a small warm FP16 buffer (idle host) for critical long-context routes to avoid user-facing 10s spikes.

[00:05:15] Lisa: How about calibration? You mentioned per-channel clipping. Can that reduce FP8 brittleness?

[00:05:20] Diego: Yes. For FP8 we experimented with three calibrations: global scale, layerwise clip, and per-channel activation clipping. Per-channel reduced extreme tails but didn't remove all late-output drift. Additional tricks: mixed-precision within a single model (keep certain layers in FP16), bias correction and small fine-tune (LLM dequantization fine tune) — the latter reduced error rates but adds cost/time.

[00:05:50] Maya: If fine-tune helps, what's the effort? A few epochs on in-domain data?

[00:05:54] Diego: For the experiments we tried a 3-epoch lightweight fine-tune on 50k in-domain examples — it improved acceptability for FP8 by ~1.5 points but didn't remove sign-flip class errors. We want to run a bigger targeted run next week.

[00:06:10] Ava: Also worth noting: runner-level operator selection matters. Our runtime picks different GEMM kernels for FP8 vs INT8 and quantized KV cache serialization is slightly different, so small implementation differences can explain some noise. We'll attach the kernel selection log.

[00:06:28] Omar: For compliance we need audit logs of any fallback events — can Redwood surface those?

[00:06:33] Jen (CSM): Yes, Console provides token-level route traces and an event stream you can pipe to your SIEM. We'll show the export steps in the follow-up doc.

[00:06:44] Maya: Good. On the business side, what's the expected cost delta if we go FP8 for 30% of traffic?

[00:06:50] Ava: Rough napkin: per-token infra cost drops by ~30-45% when moving FP16->FP8 depending on batch utilization and caching. So at 30% traffic you'd expect ~10-15% overall cost reduction. We'll send a more precise delta with pricing bands.

[00:07:10] Diego: One more datapoint: under adversarial prompts we saw more instability in FP8 — we think dynamic exponent scaling makes it more sensitive to outlier activations. INT8 behaved more predictably but conservative.

[00:07:26] Ethan: Any thoughts on additional telemetry we should enable?

[00:07:30] Diego: Collect token-level perplexity, stop-token frequency, repetition score, and a small set of business rule checks (e.g., numeric consistency check for financial outputs). Also collect logits delta between FP16 and quant runs for a sample of requests.

[00:07:46] Maya: We'll provide the numeric-check rules. Also we want a human QA batch for long-context cases — 1k to 3k tokens.

[00:07:55] Ava: Great. So concrete plan: Diego runs a 10k prompt stability sweep on FP8 with per-channel clip + a small fine-tune variant; outputs: acceptability CSV, sample failures, logits traces. We'll then reconcile and decide whether to widen canary.

[00:08:10] Lisa: Timeline?

[00:08:12] Diego: We can run the FP8 stability sweep in 3 business days if we have the labeled prompts — results by 2025-04-18. Fine-tune run needs extra infra and 3–4 days.

[00:08:24] Maya: Sounds good. Also please include which prompts triggered the largest delta so we can audit downstream UX impacts.

[00:08:30] Samir: Will do — we'll annotate each failure w/ severity: minor (stylistic), moderate (fact flip but recoverable), critical (wrong sign/numeric).

[00:08:40] Ava: Any blockers?

[00:08:44] Omar: We need the security checklist and KMS integration doc before we enable a dedicated FP8 pool for our account.

[00:08:50] Jen: We'll attach the KMS checklist and Valley of Compliance doc in the follow-up email — link posted in chat (link: https://redwood.example.com/sec/kms-checklist).

[00:08:58] Maya: One last Q — are there model variants we can fall back to that are quant-friendly but less brittle? Like a distilled INT8 variant?

[00:09:06] Diego: Yes, we have quant-friendly model variants: INT8-distilled and FP16-quant-hybrid. The distillation reduces early-layer sensitivity and behaves better on numeric outputs but at some cost to fluency. It's a good candidate for long-context fallback.

[00:09:25] Ava: Ok we're almost at 40 minutes. Recap next steps: Diego to run the FP8 stability sweep and per-channel calibration, Ava to share pricing & security docs, Maya to provide 3 prompt templates + 200 labeled QA examples, and Jen to share the KMS checklist. We'll reconvene next week same time.

[00:09:47] Lisa: Thanks everyone.

[00:09:50] (call ends)

Notes/addenda: Shared artifacts referenced — performance spreadsheet (link: https://redwood.example.com/pilot/aperture-week2-bench.csv), sample failure doc (drive link in chat), and the KMS checklist above. Transcript contains occasional transcription issues: "KV cash" vs "KV cache", some Proper nouns mangled.

End of transcript.
